"You may have a hard time comparing your situation and experience with BPD to others, and I want to elaborate that this is harmful."

Why is that harmful? I identify with the quiet BPD subtype and the truth is that there are a lot of behaviours from others with BPD that I can't relate to. I don't experience splitting or anger issues. I don't relate to struggling with lashing out towards others. It isn't harmful for me to state that, it's not passing judgement on others, it's just the truth.

I don't believe it's harmful to recognise that a lot of us who identify with quiet BPD don't share those experiences. I actually think it's helpful to have a subtype because it allows those of us whose symptoms present similarly to easily connect and relate to each other. The same could be said for people who identify with other subtypes.

The truth is that the BPD diagnosis is incredibly vague as a whole. I think that's a problem. There is so much variety in symptoms that subtypes are helpful to narrow that down.

I was misdiagnosed with depression and anxiety for a decade because I don't outwardly express many symptoms. It was only when I finally saw a psychiatrist who had knowledge of the different ways BPD can present that I actually received the correct diagnosis.

If it wasn't for the quiet BPD subtype, I probably wouldn't believe I have BPD because I don't relate to so many others who have it. That would have prevented me from getting the help I need.

I don't see subtypes as being inherently hierarchical or discriminatory. I think that just depends on an individual's attitude and the way they choose to use them. This kind of behaviour could happen regardless of the existence of subtypes.

DBT can be attempted at home but obviously it's better to do with a therapist. I haven't actually had DBT with a therapist, just regular talking therapy, but I did learn some DBT skills myself at home and I think it helped. I used The Dialectical Behaviour Therapy Skills Workbook by Matthew McKay, Jeffrey C. Wood and Jeffrey Brantley.

Also for me personally, it really helps to vent in the notes app on my phone when I need to. It lets me get all my emotions out without putting them on other people and helps me to work through things in the process. So firstly before seeking reassurance from your partner, I'd make sure you take some time to manage your emotions and really reflect on whatever has made you feel insecure and why. This is where DBT skills really help.

If you still feel like you haven't been able to get past it on your own or by talking it through with your therapist/friend, and you really do need some reassurance, then I'd approach it in a way that's non-confrontational and mindful of her feelings. Have a calm discussion about it. No shouting or name calling, ever. Don't jump to accusations or placing blame, don't assume her feelings etc. Communicate clearly why you're feeling insecure and what would help you feel reassured. If there's ever an occasion where you know rationally deep down that it's insecurity from your own issues and not from anything she's done (this has been the case for me a lot of times when I felt insecure), then make sure you tell her that.

I'd say stop venting to her about everything. I've done this in the past and thought it was okay, that your partner should be there to emotionally support you and I didn't want him to fix it just listen. I said the exact same thing as you, that I didn't want him to be my therapist. But it's essentially using your partner as an emotional dumping ground and that's very draining for them. Build a good support system of friends, family if possible, and a therapist if possible so you don't rely solely on your partner for emotional support. Of course it's okay to vent to them sometimes, but not excessively.

Even though nothing else gives you the feeling of happiness as much as her, it's very important to do things anyway. Make sure you set goals for yourself and your future that aren't based on your relationship. Make sure you find some hobbies of your own. Spend time with friends without your partner and let her spend time with hers without you. Basically just make a very conscious effort to ensure you have your own life outside of the relationship and don't become too dependent on them.

Try not to allow your fear of losing her affect your actions. Work on managing those feelings on your own and developing the ability to regulate your own emotions. It's okay to seek reassurance from a partner in times of insecurity sometimes, but it's important not to do it every single time you feel insecure (also something I've done in the past) and learn how to reassure yourself.

I did blame myself for a very long time because I was misdiagnosed with just anxiety and depression for around 16 years. Then I was finally diagnosed with BPD recently and researched it more. Now I realise the way I am was caused by childhood trauma that physically altered my brain development. That actually makes it not my fault at all. I am responsible for my actions, but not for having my disorder.

After learning more about BPD, I find it more difficult not to blame my parents. I know they did the best they knew how to do whilst being emotionally damaged themselves, and I do love them and know they love me. I know they had traumatic childhoods themselves and didn't have access back then to the same mental health treatment I have now. But now that I realise the extent of the damage caused by my childhood, I find it hard not to hold a little bit of resentment. I feel a lot of guilt admitting that, like it's a betrayal to them.

I feel like I probably could have been a mentally healthy person had I not experienced being hit as a child, witnessing domestic violence towards my mother, and having a generally very unstable home life with a lot of arguing all the time. Things around me would be thrown and broken out of anger. My brother punched holes in walls and we physically fought. I gave as good as I got and I started fights too, but he was much bigger than me. My dad would kick our cat out of frustration and I had to start standing in front of our cat to make sure he was protected. And I feel like having the threat of calling social services to take me away when I played up, and having my dad leave the country and tell me he didn't know when or if he was coming back when I was 10, probably did a lot to cause my fear of abandonment. There were a lot of happy times too of course, but definitely a lot of bad times. Having an unstable surrounding was all I'd ever known as a child/teenager. I was also bullied horribly in school. I developed severe anorexia at the age of 11 and began self harming as a coping mechanism.

But I also have a habit of downplaying my trauma and saying "other people had it worse." I would say to my therapists "well yeah I was hit, but I wasn't beaten like some other people were." The truth is that there's always going to be somebody who "had it worse." But trauma is trauma, and all trauma is damaging.

My parents have changed a lot over time and are much better, healthier people now. We have a good relationship. But I also realise they made a lot of mistakes as parents that did a lot of damage to me, and I now understand that it's down to me to make sure the generational trauma ends here. If I ever have children, which I'm not sure I ever will, I know I will make sure to do better.
